note.question: How should a health system report first-stage screening results when the information itself changes whether high-risk patients adhere to the recommended diagnostic follow-up?
note.overview: The health system commits to a signaling rule by selecting screening cutoffs, patients update Bayesian beliefs from the resulting signal and strategically decide whether to take a colonoscopy, and the system anticipates those best responses. This is an applied Bayesian-persuasion/information-design game.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: The health system first commits to the number and values of FIT cutoffs, which map fecal-hemoglobin readings and latent health states into reported outcomes. Each individual observes the test outcome, updates objective and subjective beliefs about polyps and cancer, observes own follow-up disutility, and chooses whether to undergo colonoscopy. The health system's design anticipates these adherence probabilities. The cutoff is a signaling mechanism rather than only a diagnostic threshold.

components.label: Equilibrium or solution concept
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Committed Bayesian-persuasion solution with patient follow-up best responses. The health system chooses an MLR-feasible signal structure while each receiver follows up exactly when the information-avoidance random utility difference is positive. Theorem 1 proves a minimum-cutoff dichotomous test optimal for follow-up maximization under joint concavity; Theorem 2 proves full continuous reporting optimal for effectiveness maximization under joint convexity and monotonicity.
